subject: ENGLISH LANGUAGE
title: Reading: Intensive Reading (Dialogue)
overview: A dialogue is a conversation written so that each speaker has a name and words to say. In this sub-strand you will read dialogues about email and the internet, find new words, answer factual and inferential questions, and put the events in a logical order.

lessons.title: How a dialogue is written
objectives: Use the speaker's name to follow who is talking.
Find new words and notice a repeated sentence pattern.
Read a short dialogue aloud with a partner.
lessons.intro: In a story, the narrator does a lot of the telling. In a dialogue, the speakers do it themselves. If you lose track of the names, you will give one person's idea to somebody else.
lessons.notes:
### The parts you can see
A dialogue is set out in lines. Each line begins with the speaker's name, then the words that person says. There are no long descriptions between the lines in the dialogues you will read here. You work out the place and the feelings from what the speakers say.

New words are often explained by the next line. If a character asks what a word means, read the answer before you skip ahead.

### Dialogue: The First Message
NEMA: Uncle, what is an email?
JUMA: An email is a message we send through the internet.
NEEMA: How do I send one to my mother?
JUMA: First we click Compose. Then we type her email address. It has her name, the sign @, and the service that keeps her mail.
NEEMA: Where will she see it?
JUMA: In her inbox. Our message waits in the outbox until it goes. After that, we can save a copy.
NEEMA: May I search for a game as well?
JUMA: Not in this lesson. We came to send one message. We do not click links we do not know, and we do not type our password for anyone.

### Words and patterns
New words: email, compose, address, inbox, outbox, save, search, click, password.

Notice the sentence pattern First we... Then we... Juma uses it to give steps in order. You can reuse that pattern when you explain a task.

When you read aloud, change your voice a little for each speaker. Keep the words exact. Do not add a joke that is not in the line, because you may change a safety instruction.

keyWords.meaning: a written conversation in which each speaker's words are shown
the person who says a line in a dialogue
a secret word or phrase that lets only the right person open an account

examples.problem: Who explains what an email is?
steps: Find the question 'what is an email?'
Read the next speaker's line.

examples.problem: What sentence pattern does Juma use for the steps?
steps: Look at the line that begins with First.
The next step begins with Then.

activity.title: Two voices
materials: A printed copy of The First Message
steps: Underline every speaker's name.
Circle three words that are new to you and write a meaning from the dialogue.
With a partner, read the dialogue aloud. Swap parts and read it again.
Find the First, Then pattern and use it to tell your partner how to drink a glass of water safely, as a practice of the pattern only.

practice.question: Where does Juma say the mother's message will appear?
What waits in the outbox?
practice.answer: The message they have written, until it is sent.

practice.question: Why does Juma refuse the game during the lesson?
practice.answer: They came to send one message, and he wants them to stay on that task and avoid unknown links.

summary: A speaker's name shows whose words you are reading.
The next line often explains a new word.
First and Then show the order of steps.

lessons.title: Facts and inferences
objectives: Answer a factual question by pointing to the line that says it.
Answer an inferential question by using clues from the dialogue.
Tell a fact and an inference apart.
lessons.intro: Some answers sit in the dialogue in plain words. Others are hidden in the way a character acts. Both kinds of reading are useful, and they are not the same skill.
lessons.notes:
### Two kinds of question
A factual question asks for a detail the dialogue states. You can point to the line. Who spoke? What did the message promise? Where were the children?

An inferential question asks you to work something out. The dialogue may not say 'Baraka was unsure', but if he stops and asks for help, you can infer that he does not want to decide alone. An inference must follow the clues. It is not a wild guess, and it is not a new fact you invent.

### Dialogue: The Prize That Was Not a Prize
BARAKA: I have a new message in my inbox.
CHEBET: Who sent it?
BARAKA: I do not know the address. It says I have won a phone if I click a link and send my home address.
CHEBET: Stop. Do not click. Let us call the teacher.
TEACHER: You were right to wait. We do not open links from people we do not know. We do not send our home address, our school details or our password in an email.
BARAKA: I felt ready to click because the prize sounded exciting. I will ask you first next time.
TEACHER: A real prize does not arrive from a stranger who demands your address. Close that message. We will compose a short email to your father about the class project instead.

### Sample questions
Factual: What did the strange message promise? A phone, if Baraka clicked and sent his home address.
Factual: What three things does the teacher say not to send or do? Do not open unknown links. Do not send a home address, school details or a password.

Inferential: Why did Chebet say 'Stop' so quickly? She heard two danger signs together: an unknown sender and a request for a home address.
Inferential: How had Baraka felt before Chebet spoke? He says the prize sounded exciting and he felt ready to click, so he was tempted, not certain.

If a question says 'according to the teacher', quote the idea from the teacher's lines. If a question says 'why do you think', use clues and begin with 'I think... because...'

keyWords.meaning: a question whose answer is stated in the text
a question whose answer you work out from clues
a detail that helps you work something out
a word or button on a screen that opens another page or file when you click it

examples.problem: Is this factual or inferential: 'What prize did the message promise?'
steps: Look for words that state the prize.
Baraka says the message offers a phone.
examples.answer: Factual. The answer is a phone.

examples.problem: Why is the teacher's last plan safer than the strange message?
steps: The strange message is from an unknown sender and asks for a home address.
The new email is to Baraka's father, someone he knows, about a class project.
examples.answer: It goes to a known person and does not ask Baraka to give away private information.

activity.title: Point to the line
materials: Copies of The Prize That Was Not a Prize
steps: Read the dialogue silently, then aloud in groups of three.
Write two factual questions and two inferential questions.
Swap with another group. Answer their questions. For a fact, underline the line in one colour. For an inference, write the clue in the other colour.
Reject any inference that the lines do not support.

practice.question: What does the strange message ask Baraka to send?
practice.answer: His home address, after clicking a link.

practice.question: Give one clue that Chebet thinks the message is unsafe.
practice.answer: She says 'Stop. Do not click.' as soon as she hears that the sender is unknown and wants a home address.

practice.question: Why is 'Baraka won a phone' not a fact from this dialogue?
practice.answer: The message claims it, but the teacher explains that a stranger demanding an address is not a real prize. Baraka does not receive a phone.

practice.question: Write one inferential question about the teacher's feelings.
practice.answer: Why is the teacher pleased? A good answer notes that she says they were right to wait. The question itself should ask something the text does not say in a single label.

summary: A fact can be pointed to in a line.
An inference uses clues and must fit the dialogue.
An exciting promise from an unknown sender is a reason to stop, not to click.

lessons.title: Events in a logical order
objectives: List the events of a dialogue in the order they happen.
Notice when a later line depends on an earlier one.
Explain why reading for comprehension is worth doing more than once.
lessons.intro: If you retell a dialogue backwards, the careful choice looks like an accident. Order is part of the meaning. Baraka calls the teacher because Chebet warns him, not the other way round.
lessons.notes:
### Why order matters
Intensive reading means reading closely for exact meaning. One close-reading job is to track events. Each line can cause the next.

In The Prize That Was Not a Prize the order is:

1. Baraka sees a new message in the inbox.
2. Chebet asks who sent it.
3. Baraka says the sender is unknown and the message promises a phone.
4. Chebet tells him not to click and to call the teacher.
5. The teacher praises the wait and states the rules.
6. Baraka admits he had felt ready to click.
7. The teacher tells him to close the message and helps him write to his father instead.

Step 7 only makes sense after step 5. You cannot understand the safe email unless you know they rejected the strange one.

### A second dialogue
Read this shorter conversation and number the events yourself.

AWUOR: The computer lab is free. May I check the inbox?
MR OTIENO: Yes. I will sit with you.
AWUOR: My cousin has replied. She asks for the date of the music festival.
MR OTIENO: That reply is from someone you know. Read it first. Then we can compose an answer and click Send.
AWUOR: I will type the date and nothing private. I will not send my password.
MR OTIENO: Good. Save a copy before we leave the lab.

Events: they enter the lab; the teacher agrees to stay; Awuor finds a known reply; they decide to answer with only the date; they will save a copy. The promise about the password belongs with the reply, not at the beginning.

### Reading again for a purpose
The first reading gives you the story. The second reading can hunt for one thing: new words, facts, or the order of events. That is why comprehension improves when you read with a purpose instead of sliding your eyes down the page once.

Keep this habit outside the lesson. Instructions, news and messages all reward a second look. On the internet, that second look includes a safety question: do I know who sent this, and should an adult see it before I click?

keyWords.meaning: an order in which each event follows sensibly from the one before
reading carefully to understand exact information

examples.problem: Which comes first: Baraka admits he wanted to click, or Chebet says stop?
steps: Find both lines.
Chebet's warning comes before Baraka explains his feeling to the teacher.

examples.problem: Why can Awuor reply to her cousin when Baraka should not reply to the prize message?
steps: Compare the senders.
The cousin is known and asks for a date. The prize sender is unknown and asks for a home address.
examples.answer: Awuor knows her cousin and an adult is beside her. Baraka does not know the sender, and the message asks for private information.

activity.title: Order the events
materials: Sentence strips of the seven events from the prize dialogue, mixed up
steps: In groups, put the event strips in logical order without looking, then check against the dialogue.
Do the same for Awuor's lab conversation, writing the events in your own short sentences.
Each learner chooses a purpose for a second reading: new words, facts or order. Report one finding.
Say one reason you would read a message twice before clicking anything.

practice.question: List the first two events in The Prize That Was Not a Prize.
practice.answer: Baraka sees a new message. Chebet asks who sent it.

practice.question: What does Awuor decide to type in her reply?
practice.answer: The date of the music festival, and nothing private. She will not send her password.

practice.question: What is one purpose for reading a dialogue a second time?
practice.answer: To collect new words, to check facts, or to confirm the order of events.

practice.question: Why does step 7 in the prize dialogue depend on the teacher?
practice.answer: The teacher is the one who tells Baraka to close the strange message and to write to his father instead.

summary: Events in a dialogue follow one another for a reason.
A second reading can focus on words, facts or order.
Knowing the sender, and having an adult nearby, changes what it is safe to answer.

quiz.question: In a dialogue, the name at the start of a line tells you
quiz.explanation: Each line is labelled with its speaker.

quiz.question: Juma says a new email is started by clicking
quiz.explanation: He tells Neema to click Compose first.

quiz.question: A factual answer is one that
options: you invent to make the story exciting
the dialogue states and you can point to
quiz.explanation: Facts are written in the lines.

quiz.question: The strange message promised Baraka
options: a phone if he clicked and sent his home address
a new keyboard from the teacher
quiz.explanation: Baraka reads that promise from the unknown address.

quiz.question: Chebet's quick 'Stop' supports the inference that she
options: thought the unknown message was unsafe
quiz.explanation: She reacts as soon as she hears the unknown sender and the request for an address.

quiz.question: Which action fits a message from a stranger who wants your password?
options: Send your home address to be polite
Do not click, and tell a trusted adult
Forward it to the whole class for fun
quiz.explanation: The teacher gives this safety rule in the dialogue.

quiz.question: Which event happens last in the prize dialogue?
options: The teacher suggests an email to his father and closing the strange message
Baraka says he does not know the address
quiz.explanation: The safe plan comes after the warning and the teacher's rule.

quiz.question: Awuor may answer her cousin because
options: she knows the sender and an adult is with her
the cousin asked for a password
quiz.explanation: Mr Otieno stays with her, and the cousin is known. She still avoids private details.

quiz.question: Reading a dialogue twice can help you
quiz.explanation: A second reading with a purpose improves comprehension.

quiz.question: Write the next event after Chebet says not to click.
quiz.answer: They call the teacher, and the teacher explains the rules.
quiz.explanation: Chebet's warning leads directly to fetching the teacher.
